# Zeek Documentation

This is the documentation for Zeek, hosted at [https://docs.zeek.org](https://docs.zeek.org).

Zeek's documentation is a [Read the Docs][read the docs] [Sphinx][Sphinx] project, found at [rtd-docs][rtd-docs].

Zeek's documentation style guide can be found [here](https://github.com/zeek/zeek/wiki/Documentation-Style-and-Conventions).

## Source-Tree Organization

The documentation has a top-level `conf.py` file for any Sphinx configuration. Add documentation by adding a new file, then referencing it within a `toctree` (or Table of Contents Tree).

Zeek's documentation uses a custom domain from `ext/zeek.py`. This adds some reStructuredText (reST) directives like `:zeek:see:` which are used throughout. This is primarily when linking to Zeek's auto-generated documentation via Zeekygen. This auto-generated documentation mostly lives under the `scripts/` directory, or its file name starts with "autogenerated." Changes to any auto-generated documentation should go in the corresponding file in the parent Zeek directory. For example, in order to edit documentation from `scripts/base/init-bare.zeek.rst`, you should edit the file `../scripts/base/init-bare.zeek` (relative from the `doc` directory).

## Generating Zeekygen Reference Docs

Zeekygen docs are generated from the top-level Zeek directory. You must build Zeek from source first, so read through [the building from scratch](https://docs.zeek.org/en/current/building-from-source.html) section to build Zeek. Then, run Zeek's `update-zeekygen-docs.sh`:

```bash
../ci/update-zeekygen-docs.sh
```

Now, you can preview the changes to make sure they are okay.

> [!NOTE]
> Zeek automatically generates this documentation (via `../.github/workflows/generate-docs.yml`), so it often is not necessary to commit the changed files. Depending on your configuration, the generated files may differ (particularly, AF_Packet will not generate on MacOS).

## Building the Documentation

First make sure you have the required dependencies used for building docs:

  * **Python interpreter** \>= 3.10
  * **Sphinx**: [https://www.sphinx-doc.org/en/master/](https://www.sphinx-doc.org/en/master/)
  * **Read the Docs Sphinx Theme**: [https://github.com/readthedocs/sphinx\_rtd\_theme](https://github.com/readthedocs/sphinx_rtd_theme)
  * **GitPython**: [https://github.com/gitpython-developers/GitPython](https://github.com/gitpython-developers/GitPython)

If you have [pip][pip], you may just use the command `pip3 install -r requirements.txt` to install all the dependencies using the `requirements.txt`.

Now run `make` within this directory. After the build completes, HTML documentation is symlinked in `build/html` and you can open the `index.html` found there in your web browser.

There's also a `make livehtml` (requires `pip3 install sphinx-autobuild`) target in the top-level Makefile that is useful for editing the reST files and seeing changes rendered out live to a separate browser.

## Hosting

Documentation is hosted by [Read the Docs][Read the Docs] (RTD). The web-interface is accessible via the [zeek-docs][rtd-docs] project.

The [zeek-docs][rtd-docs] project uses a combination of `.readthedocs.yml` files (found in `../.readthedocs.yml`, for example) and other settings only accessible through the web interface (like domain and subproject settings). Some caveats:

  * There is an associated, always-failing project at [https://app.readthedocs.org/projects/zeek/](https://app.readthedocs.org/projects/zeek/). It's always-failing because RTD redirects only activate when pages 404 and this project exists so that all attempts to use `https://zeek.rtfd.io` or `https://zeek.readthedocs.io` get redirected to `https://docs.zeek.org`. Those would have been the project URLs if ownership of the RTD 'zeek' project was had from the start, but it was only obtained later, after documentation already started development in the 'zeek-docs' RTD project slug.
  * Redirects are managed via an external script, found in the [zeek-aux][zeek-aux] repository, called `doc-redirects`. See the output from that script for information on how to use it. Redirects are managed in the `redirects.yml` file within the `doc` directory.
  * There are RTD subprojects for things like Broker, Package Manager, and Spicy. The use of subprojects simply allows access to their RTD docs via the custom domain of `https://docs.zeek.org`.
  * RTD will auto-build any newly-pushed commits to [zeek-docs][rtd-docs] (i.e., a webhook is configured), but if a tag is changed to point somewhere different, you'll typically have to go into the RTD web interface, "Edit" the associated version under "Versions", "wipe" the existing docs, and then manually trigger a rebuild of that version tag under "Builds".

[pip]: https://pypi.org/project/pip

This document summarizes the most important changes in the current Zeek
release. For a more detailed record, see the Git history of the corresponding
release branch.

Zeek 9.1.0
==========

We'd like to thank ... for their contributions to this release.

Breaking Changes
----------------

- With the removal of the ``&backend`` and related attributes, we determined
  that the ``zeek::broker::Manager::AdvanceTime()`` function is also unnecessary.
  It wouldn't function anymore, but it is in non-detail namespace and so this
  is a breaking API change.

- Similarly, the ``broker_backend`` field has been removed from the ``script_id``
  record type. This is the type returned by the ``global_ids()`` BIF method.

- Zeek no longer discards packets with bad IP, TCP, UDP, ICMP, or IPv6 mobility
  header checksums by default. Instead the packets will be analyzed, but the
  weirds and ``C``/``c`` flags in conn.log's history field will still be produced.

  Previously, the packets would not get analyzed. The new ``drop_bad_checksums``
  option restores the previous behavior:

	redef drop_bad_checksums = T;

  Both ``ignore_checksums`` and ``-C`` remain unchanged: Both cause checksums to
  neither be computed nor validated.

  This also means that Zeek may analyze packets that the receiving endpoint drops.

- Configuration of git checkouts now requires tags, which may not exist for forks.
  To quickly fetch tags from upstream, run the following:

	git fetch --no-recurse-submodules https://github.com/zeek/zeek.git --tags

  For other options, see the "Retrieving the Sources" section in the
  "Building from Source" instructions in the Zeek documentation.


New Functionality
-----------------

- The DHCPv6 analyzer now supports prefix delegation (IA_PD) and logs
  assigned prefixes in ``dhcpv6.log`` via the ``assigned_prefix`` field.

- Zeek now includes an initial version of a DHCPv6 analyzer, producing ``dhcpv6.log``.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Generate a DHCP trace exercising option 55/60 fingerprinting and clusters.

The trace contains four DHCPDISCOVER messages from three clients.  Each
message carries a vendor class identifier (option 60) and a parameter request
list (option 55).  The first two clients request the same options in the same
order and therefore share a DHCP fingerprint, while the third client uses two
different parameter request lists of its own.  This lets the fingerprinting
regression test verify both the per-message ``dhcp_fingerprint`` field and the
grouping of clients into fingerprint clusters.

Written with OpenAI Codex using Scapy.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from pathlib import Path

from scapy.all import BOOTP, DHCP, IP, UDP, Ether, wrpcap

BASE_TIME = 1_700_000_000.0

# (client MAC, transaction id, parameter request list, vendor class id)
MESSAGES = [
    (
        "02:00:00:00:00:01",
        0x10000001,
        [1, 3, 6, 15, 31, 33, 43, 44, 46, 47, 119, 252],
        "MSFT 5.0",
    ),
    (
        "02:00:00:00:00:02",
        0x10000002,
        [1, 3, 6, 15, 31, 33, 43, 44, 46, 47, 119, 252],
        "MSFT 5.0",
    ),
    (
        "02:00:00:00:00:03",
        0x10000003,
        [1, 3, 6, 15, 119, 252],
        "android-dhcp-13",
    ),
    (
        "02:00:00:00:00:03",
        0x10000004,
        [1, 3, 6, 12, 15, 28, 42],
        "android-dhcp-13",
    ),
]


def dhcp_discover(mac, xid, param_list, vendor_class, ts):
    bootp = BOOTP(
        op=1,
        htype=1,
        hlen=6,
        hops=0,
        xid=xid,
        flags=0x8000,
        chaddr=mac,
    )
    pkt = (
        Ether(src=mac, dst="ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff")
        / IP(src="0.0.0.0", dst="255.255.255.255")
        / UDP(sport=68, dport=67)
        / bootp
        / DHCP(
            options=[
                ("message-type", "discover"),
                ("param_req_list", param_list),
                ("vendor_class_id", vendor_class),
                "end",
            ]
        )
    )
    pkt.time = ts
    return pkt


def main():
    packets = [
        dhcp_discover(mac, xid, param_list, vendor_class, BASE_TIME + index * 0.001)
        for index, (mac, xid, param_list, vendor_class) in enumerate(MESSAGES)
    ]
    wrpcap(str(Path(__file__).with_suffix("")), packets)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

+DHCP Fingerprinting
+===================
+
+DHCP clients tell servers a good deal about themselves in the options of
+their DHCPDISCOVER and DHCPREQUEST messages. Two options are particularly
+useful for endpoint fingerprinting:
+
+- Option 55, the *parameter request list*, is an ordered list of the DHCP
+  option codes the client would like the server to return. Different
+  operating systems and DHCP client implementations request different
+  options in different orders, so this list is a stable and widely used
+  fingerprinting signal.
+- Option 60, the *vendor class identifier*, is a string that often names
+  the vendor or operating system family, such as ``MSFT 5.0`` for a
+  Microsoft client or an ``android-dhcp-*`` value for an Android device.
+
+Zeek logs the raw option 60 string in the ``vendor_class`` field and the
+raw option 55 list in the ``param_request_list`` field of :file:`dhcp.log`.
+It additionally derives a compact textual fingerprint from the parameter
+request list in the ``dhcp_fingerprint`` field. The fingerprint is the
+comma-separated concatenation of the requested option codes, preserving
+the client's ordering:
+
+.. literal-emph::
+
+  1,3,6,15,31,33,43,44,46,47,119,252
+
+Two clients that produce the same fingerprint request the same DHCP
+options in the same order and typically belong to the same operating
+system or device family. The
+:zeek:see:`policy/protocols/dhcp/fingerprint-clusters` policy script
+groups clients by this fingerprint. Loading it adds a
+:file:`dhcp_fp_cluster.log` with one record per distinct fingerprint,
+including the set of client MAC addresses observed with it and the number
+of distinct clients in the cluster:
+
+::
+
+  {
+    "ts": "2023-11-14T22:13:20.000000Z",
+    "dhcp_fingerprint": "1,3,6,15,31,33,43,44,46,47,119,252",
+    "num_clients": 2,
+    "client_macs": [
+      "02:00:00:00:00:01",
+      "02:00:00:00:00:02"
+    ]
+  }
+
+The policy also raises a :zeek:see:`DHCP::new_fingerprint_cluster_member`
+event each time a new client MAC joins a cluster, and the clusters remain
+available at runtime in the :zeek:see:`DHCP::fingerprint_clusters` table.
+
 Conclusion
 ==========
*** End Patch

New Functionality
-----------------

- The DHCPv6 analyzer now supports prefix delegation (IA_PD) and logs
  assigned prefixes in ``dhcpv6.log`` via the ``assigned_prefix`` field.

- Zeek now includes an initial version of a DHCPv6 analyzer, producing ``dhcpv6.log``.

  The analyzer implementation and ``dhcpv6.log`` are in early stages and will be
  actively iterated on and likely changed towards the Zeek 10.0 release. If you
  have opinions and use-cases about the structure of the log and hooks or additional
  events, please get in touch and let us know!

  To disable the analyzer in case of issues, use the following snippet:

	redef Analyzer::disabled_analyzers += {
		Analyzer::ANALYZER_DHCPV6,
	};

- The SSH DPD signature now matches on ``SSH-`` rather than ``SSH-[12]`` to catch
  tools using unconventional SSH version strings.

- The supported SSH KEX methods are now configurable via a new script-level
  table ``SSH::kex_methods`` to allow updating the mapping without the need
  to adapt analyzer source code and recompile Zeek.

- The input framework now supports optional records in its input files. The
  fields of absent records, including potential nested records, should be
  listed with the configured ``Input::unset_field`` character (normally "-").

- The systemd-generator now places worker processes into interface specific slices
  named after the interface section name.

#!/bin/bash
# Repair submodules left at wrong/broken revisions by aborted shallow clones.
set -u
cd /home/dev/feedback/uid21951

git submodule status --recursive | while read -r state rest; do
    # fields: <sha> <path> (...)
    sha=$(echo "$rest" | awk '{print $1}')
    path=$(echo "$rest" | awk '{print $2}')
    case "$state" in
        -*) mark="missing" ;;
        +*) mark="wrong" ;;
        *) continue ;;
    esac
    echo "=== repairing $path ($mark -> $sha)"
    if [ ! -d "$path" ]; then
        echo "no dir $path, skipping"
        continue
    fi
    (
        cd "$path" || exit 1
        git fetch -q origin "$sha" || { echo "fetch failed $path"; exit 1; }
        git checkout -q "$sha" || { echo "checkout failed $path"; exit 1; }
        echo "ok $path"
    ) || exit 1
done
echo "REPAIR-ALL-DONE"

#!/bin/bash
# Robustly repair every submodule (including nested ones) by fetching and
# checking out exactly the gitlink SHA recorded in the superproject tree.
set -u
ROOT=/home/dev/feedback/uid21951
cd "$ROOT"

# Emit "path sha" for every gitlink reachable from HEAD, recursively.
mapfile -t entries < <(git ls-tree -r HEAD | awk '$2=="commit" {print $4" "$3}')

for entry in "${entries[@]}"; do
    path="${entry%% *}"
    sha="${entry##* }"
    [ -d "$path" ] || { echo "MISSING-DIR $path"; continue; }
    (
        cd "$ROOT/$path" || exit 1
        cur=$(git rev-parse HEAD 2>/dev/null || echo "")
        if [ "$cur" = "$sha" ]; then
            echo "ok-already $path"
            exit 0
        fi
        git fetch -q origin "$sha" || { echo "FETCH-FAIL $path"; exit 1; }
        git checkout -q "$sha" || { echo "CHECKOUT-FAIL $path"; exit 1; }
        now=$(git rev-parse HEAD)
        [ "$now" = "$sha" ] && echo "fixed $path" || echo "MISMATCH $path"
    ) || exit 1
done
echo "REPAIR-ALL-OK"

policy/protocols/dhcp/fingerprint-clusters.zeek
===============================================
.. zeek:namespace:: DHCP

Group DHCP clients into clusters based on their option 55 parameter
request list fingerprint.  The base DHCP analyzer stores each client's
fingerprint in the ``dhcp_fingerprint`` field of :file:`dhcp.log`.
This policy script additionally maintains, for each distinct
fingerprint, the set of client hardware addresses (MACs) observed
with it in the :zeek:see:`DHCP::fingerprint_clusters` table and writes
the updated cluster to :file:`dhcp_fp_cluster.log` each time a new
client hardware address joins it.
Clients sharing a fingerprint request the same DHCP options in the
same order and typically belong to the same operating system or
device family, which makes the clusters useful for endpoint
fingerprinting.

policy/protocols/dhcp/fingerprint-clusters.zeek
===============================================
.. zeek:namespace:: DHCP

Group DHCP clients into clusters based on their option 55 parameter
request list fingerprint.  The base DHCP analyzer stores each client's
fingerprint in the ``dhcp_fingerprint`` field of :file:`dhcp.log`.
This policy script additionally maintains, for each distinct
fingerprint, the set of client hardware addresses (MACs) observed
with it in the :zeek:see:`DHCP::fingerprint_clusters` table and writes
the updated cluster to :file:`dhcp_fp_cluster.log` each time a new
client hardware address joins it.
Clients sharing a fingerprint request the same DHCP options in the
same order and typically belong to the same operating system or
device family, which makes the clusters useful for endpoint
fingerprinting.

DHCP Fingerprinting
===================

DHCP clients tell servers a good deal about themselves in the options of
their DHCPDISCOVER and DHCPREQUEST messages. Two options are particularly
useful for endpoint fingerprinting:

- Option 55, the *parameter request list*, is an ordered list of the DHCP
  option codes the client would like the server to return. Different
  operating systems and DHCP client implementations request different
  options in different orders, so this list is a stable and widely used
  fingerprinting signal.
- Option 60, the *vendor class identifier*, is a string that often names
  the vendor or operating system family, such as ``MSFT 5.0`` for a
  Microsoft client or an ``android-dhcp-*`` value for an Android device.

Zeek logs the raw option 60 string in the ``vendor_class`` field and the
raw option 55 list in the ``param_request_list`` field of :file:`dhcp.log`.
It additionally derives a compact textual fingerprint from the parameter
request list in the ``dhcp_fingerprint`` field. The fingerprint is the
comma-separated concatenation of the requested option codes, preserving
the client's ordering:

.. literal-emph::

  1,3,6,15,31,33,43,44,46,47,119,252

Two clients that produce the same fingerprint request the same DHCP
options in the same order and typically belong to the same operating
system or device family. The
:zeek:see:`policy/protocols/dhcp/fingerprint-clusters` policy script
groups clients by this fingerprint. Loading it adds a
:file:`dhcp_fp_cluster.log`. A record is written each time a new client
hardware address joins a cluster, so a fingerprint observed on multiple
clients produces several records whose ``client_macs`` set and
``num_clients`` grow over time. The current clusters also remain available
at runtime in the :zeek:see:`DHCP::fingerprint_clusters` table. For
example, the second Microsoft client joining the shared fingerprint
produces:

::

  {
    "ts": "2023-11-14T22:13:20.000000Z",
    "dhcp_fingerprint": "1,3,6,15,31,33,43,44,46,47,119,252",
    "num_clients": 2,
    "client_macs": [
      "02:00:00:00:00:01",
      "02:00:00:00:00:02"
    ]
  }

The policy also raises a :zeek:see:`DHCP::new_fingerprint_cluster_member`
event each time a new client MAC joins a cluster.
